name: Koro
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Geissler, Christopher. 2013. Towards a Phonetic Description of Koro. BA thesis (Linguistics), Swarthmore College. 61 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/10066/10902(open repository:https://scholarship.tricolib.brynmawr.edu/handle/10066/10902)
catalog_locator: Section 4.5 'Suprasegmental phenomena', pp. 38-39 (section heading on p. 37)
catalog_quote: However, in the Koro dataset, no minimal pairs are present that are distinguished by tone, stress, or accent. Some homophones do exist, as in the case of [ku] 'soil' and [ku] 'dried bamboo,' but the number of such words is small. For this and other possible homophones/minimal pairs, I observed pitch contours and measured the minimum, maximum, and median pitches of each vowel, as well as its intensity and length, but was unable to find any significant differences (see Appendix). In addition, for a number of two-syllable words, the Koro consultant would place stress on one syllable, then stress the other syllable when asked to repeat the word. Thus, with the information available, I have found no evidence for a phonemic tone, stress, or pitch-accent system in Koro.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source finds no phonemic stress (nor tone nor pitch accent): no minimal pairs by stress/tone, no measurable pitch/intensity/duration differences among homophone candidates, and prominence on disyllables varied freely between first and second syllable across repetitions by the same speaker. It does NOT state a default (non-contrastive) stress position; the observation of variable prominence suggests no fixed word-stress locus, but the author frames this as absence of evidence from a limited isolated-word corpus.
new_statements.exceptions: None; author hedges 'with the information available'. Blench 2018 (draft wordlist) independently calls Koro 'marginally tonal' with perhaps two word melodies (Low/High), 'even these may be predictable'; Sinha 2021's F0 study of homophones is inconclusive. Neither mentions word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms only: words elicited in isolation, recordings of a single speaker (Sange Degio) from the Living Tongues/Enduring Voices Koro recordings; author explicitly excluded phrasal data. Sinha 2021 separately notes sentence-final 'stress' marking polar questions (intonational, not lexical).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: Koro (Koro Aka) of East Kameng district (Yangse/Yangsey and nearby villages), glottocode koro1316, ISO jkr — not to be confused with Hruso Aka (hrus1242), with which it was formerly lumped, nor with the several Oceanic/African languages also called Koro. Geissler's data are one speaker's (Sange Degio) isolated-word recordings from the Living Tongues Koro talking-dictionary corpus; Sinha's data are from Yangsey village speakers.

sources.quote: However, in the Koro dataset, no minimal pairs are present that are distinguished by tone, stress, or accent. Some homophones do exist, as in the case of [ku] 'soil' and [ku] 'dried bamboo,' but the number of such words is small. For this and other possible homophones/minimal pairs, I observed pitch contours and measured the minimum, maximum, and median pitches of each vowel, as well as its intensity and length, but was unable to find any significant differences (see Appendix). sources.note: Section 4.5 'Suprasegmental phenomena' (pp. 37-39): no minimal pairs distinguished by tone, stress or accent; pitch/intensity/length measurements on homophone candidates show no significant differences (Appendix B); for disyllables the consultant stressed one syllable, then the other on repetition; concludes 'no evidence for a phonemic tone, stress, or pitch accent system in Koro'. No statement of a default stress position. Data = isolated words from one speaker (Sange Degio), Enduring Voices/Living Tongues recordings.

sources.note: Chapter 2 'Phonology of Koro' (pp. 28-49) has no word-stress statement at all; section 2.3 'Homophones and Tone in Koro' (pp. 41-44) reports an inconclusive F0 study of seven homophone pairs ('does not show a possibility to distinguish tone from each other'). Only prosodic remark elsewhere: ch. 4 says polar questions are marked 'by a stress on the verb at the end of the sentence or on the final word of the sentence' (sentence-level, not word stress). Data from Yangsey village, East Kameng.
